summary: Evogliptin is an oral dipeptidyl peptidase-4 (DPP-4) inhibitor (gliptin) used for type 2 diabetes mellitus. It is NOT FDA-approved; it was developed by Dong-A ST and approved in South Korea (marketed as Suganon) in 2015, with availability in some other markets. The usual dose is 5 mg once daily. By inhibiting DPP-4 it prevents the breakdown of the incretin hormones GLP-1 and GIP, increasing glucose-dependent insulin secretion and reducing glucagon, thereby lowering fasting and post-meal glucose and improving HbA1c with a low intrinsic risk of hypoglycemia. It is used as monotherapy (with diet and exercise) or in combination with other antidiabetic agents such as metformin or SGLT2 inhibitors. As with the DPP-4 inhibitor class, important considerations include the risk of pancreatitis, hypersensitivity reactions (including rare angioedema and serious skin reactions), and severe joint pain; dosing and indications follow the applicable regional (non-US) product information.

moa: Evogliptin is a potent and highly selective inhibitor of dipeptidyl peptidase-4 (DPP-4), the enzyme that rapidly degrades the incretin hormones glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) and glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide (GIP). By inhibiting DPP-4, evogliptin increases and prolongs the levels of active GLP-1 and GIP, which - in a glucose-dependent manner - enhance insulin secretion from pancreatic beta cells and suppress glucagon secretion from alpha cells. The net effect is reduced hepatic glucose output and improved post-prandial and fasting glycemia, with a low intrinsic risk of hypoglycemia because the incretin effect is glucose-dependent. It is highly selective for DPP-4 over the related enzymes DPP-8 and DPP-9.

absolute: Known hypersensitivity to evogliptin (e.g., anaphylaxis, angioedema)
Type 1 diabetes mellitus or diabetic ketoacidosis (not appropriate therapy)
relative: Significant renal impairment (consider dosing per local label)
Concomitant sulfonylurea or insulin (hypoglycemia risk - reduce companion agent)
monitor: Glycemic control (HbA1c, fasting and post-prandial glucose)
Signs and symptoms of acute pancreatitis
Hypersensitivity reactions and severe skin reactions
Severe and disabling joint pain (DPP-4 inhibitor class effect)

preg: There are insufficient data on evogliptin use in pregnancy; it is generally not recommended. Insulin is preferred to control diabetes during pregnancy. Follow regional product guidance.
lact: There are insufficient data on the presence of evogliptin in human milk; use with caution or avoid during breastfeeding, weighing the benefits against potential risks per regional guidance.
renal: As with the DPP-4 inhibitor class, dosing in moderate to severe renal impairment may require consideration or adjustment per the local label; follow the applicable regional product information and monitor renal function.
hepatic: Use with caution in significant hepatic impairment; evogliptin undergoes hepatic metabolism. Follow regional product information for any specific recommendations.

major: No major contraindicated interactions established for the DPP-4 inhibitor class at usual doses
moderate: Sulfonylureas and insulin - increased risk of hypoglycemia; consider lowering the dose of the companion agent
Strong CYP3A4 inducers/inhibitors - may alter evogliptin exposure (consider given hepatic metabolism)
minor: No clinically significant pharmacokinetic interaction observed with empagliflozin or dapagliflozin in healthy volunteer studies
interactions.food: May be taken with or without food.
interactions.alcohol: Limit alcohol due to general effects on glycemic control and the liver.
interactions.diagnostics: Monitor HbA1c and glucose; lipase/amylase if pancreatitis is suspected.

Serious skin reactions (e.g., reported with the class)

monitoring: HbA1c (every 3 months until stable) and fasting/post-prandial glucose
Symptoms of acute pancreatitis (severe persistent abdominal pain, often radiating to the back)
New or worsening severe joint pain
Renal and hepatic function as clinically indicated
counsel: Take one tablet once daily, with or without food, along with your diet and exercise plan
This medicine alone rarely causes low blood sugar, but if combined with a sulfonylurea or insulin you may need a lower dose of those - know the symptoms of hypoglycemia
Stop the medicine and seek care for severe, persistent abdominal pain (possible pancreatitis), or for rash, swelling of the face/lips/tongue, or trouble breathing
Report severe or persistent joint pain
Keep follow-up visits for blood sugar (HbA1c) checks; tell your doctor if you are pregnant, planning pregnancy, or breastfeeding
pk: Glucose-lowering effect begins with dosing; full HbA1c effect over weeks
Orally absorbed with peak plasma concentration within a few hours
Long half-life supporting once-daily dosing (approximately 32-39 hours reported)
Once-daily dosing maintains DPP-4 inhibition over 24 hours
Store at room temperature, protected from moisture, per the regional product label
pearls: NOT FDA-approved - evogliptin (Suganon) is a DPP-4 inhibitor approved in South Korea (2015, Dong-A ST) and some other markets; usual dose 5 mg once daily
Highly selective for DPP-4 over DPP-8/DPP-9; raises active GLP-1/GIP to improve glucose-dependent insulin secretion with low intrinsic hypoglycemia risk
Class effects to watch: acute pancreatitis, hypersensitivity/angioedema, severe arthralgia, and bullous pemphigoid
Hypoglycemia mainly occurs when combined with a sulfonylurea or insulin - lower the companion agent's dose
Dosing/renal-hepatic adjustments and indications follow regional (non-US) product information
missed: If a dose is missed, take it as soon as remembered on the same day. If it is almost time for the next dose, skip the missed dose and resume the once-daily schedule; do not take two doses at once.
overdose: There is limited information on evogliptin overdose. Based on the DPP-4 inhibitor class, large overdoses are generally well tolerated; management is supportive with removal of unabsorbed drug as appropriate and monitoring/treatment of any adverse effects (including hypoglycemia if other glucose-lowering agents are involved). DPP-4 inhibitors are not expected to be efficiently removed by dialysis.
